en: The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, do you wish to hear about the limit of the lifespan of sentient beings? This is the time for this, Blessed One; this is the occasion for this, Sugata."
“If the Blessed One were to teach the limit of the lifespan of beings to the monks, having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it. Therefore, monks, listen well and attend closely;
I shall speak. “So be it, Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said this to those monks:

Āps 2. Furthermore, monks, the measure of the lifespan in the hells is one eon; however, there is premature death in the interval. Āps 3. Furthermore, monks, the measure of the lifespan among animals is one eon.
There is death in the interval. Monks, those thirty days and nights of human beings constitute one day and night for the hungry ghosts.
By that reckoning of nights and days— thirty such nights making a month, and twelve such months making a year— the lifespan of the pretas is five hundred years.
That is the measure of their lifespan. By human calculation, it is fifteen thousand years;
however, there is death in the interval.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
With their throats and lips parched, they were deeply distressed;
like towering mountains, they stood with their bodies raised high.
Covered by their own hair, with gaping mouths turned upward,
their noses resembling extremely fine needles, they are emaciated;
naked and covered by their own hair, their bodies are like skeletons.
With skulls in hand, terrible, they run about wailing;
crying out with piteous sounds, they experience painful sensations.
Having harbored mutual envy toward one another, [they suffer].
"Having committed evil deeds here, they have been reborn in the world of hungry ghosts.
"Monks, the lifespan of humans in Pūrvavideha is two hundred and fifty years;
however, there is death in the interim."
Āps 7. Monks, the lifespan of humans in Avaragodānīya is five hundred years;
there is death in the interval.
Āps 8. Monks, the lifespan of humans in Uttarakuru is one thousand years.
This is the measure; there is no death in the interval.
Āps 9. For what reason is the lifespan of the humans of Uttarakuru measured at one thousand years, and there is no death in the interval?

“Monks, the humans of Uttarakuru are without the sense of ‘mine’ and without possessions; their lifespan is fixed, and having passed away from there, they proceed toward excellence and attain rebirth in heaven in the future. For this reason, monks, the lifespan of the humans of Uttarakuru is one thousand years.”
The measure of their lifespan is such that there is no death in the interval.
Āps 11. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

Beings afflicted by the suffering of poverty long for supreme wealth; [they are] servants to others, [bound] by various [forms of] servitude. Wealthy beings possessing great riches are endowed with all enjoyments.
The virtuous, endowed with wealth, grain, and people, are served by them;
they subsist upon that which is rich in merit because they performed beautiful deeds here in this world.
That is the fruit of former giving for those who are thus in the world.
For the humans in the northern continent are without "mine-ness" and without possessions;
their garments of *kalpaduṣya* are the fruit of former generosity. 9.
For them there is neither cold nor heat, and no disease exists for them;
endowed with excellence of complexion and form—this is the fruit of former giving.
[Their rice] is unbroken, stainless, and [exquisite].
For that is the fruit of former giving in those northern continents.
A beautiful, jewel-like light always blazes for them;
that is the fruit of former giving for him who cooks their food. (11–12)
No distinction of gender exists among them;
they always eat śāli rice endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
For food is served from a single vessel, yet there is no depletion of that vessel.
As long as they do not rise from their seats, that is the fruit of their former giving.
(14) The fruits of these gourds grow back even when the branch is cut;
they enjoy them even when the seeds are removed—that is the fruit of their former giving. (15)
For them there are rivers of cool water, auspicious and possessing the eight qualities;
when drunk, it does not distress the stomach—this is the fruit of former generosity.
For them there are beautiful musical trees and indeed cloth-trees.
The fragrance-tree [is] such; that is the fruit of former giving.
Musical instruments, incense, flowers, and likewise robes—
For whatever kind of thing one desires, that very thing becomes his.
Their green meadows are soft like cotton;
that they always delight therein is the fruit of former generosity.
They play with one another, and no anger is found in them;
there is neither stinginess nor envy—this is the fruit of former generosity. (20)
If it rains for even a single moment during the first watch of the night, one becomes free from dust;
that is the fruit of former giving.
A mother does not recognize her son, for they have no sense of possession.
They do not grieve over the loss of loved ones; that is the fruit of former giving. For a mother, indeed, [even when] her own son...
from her thumb milk flows; that is the fruit of former giving.
No one weeps for them; having abandoned the dead, they depart.
Birds cleanse the island—this is the fruit of former generosity.
It is surrounded on all sides by moats and is delightful with dances and songs.
Where they delight and play—that is the fruit of former giving.
Having exhausted a human lifespan of a thousand years here, they do not die prematurely; that is the fruit of former giving. (25–26)
Having abandoned their [former] state and having acquired vast prosperity, they are not reborn among the gods; that is the fruit of their previous giving.
(GBM 1705.4) Monks, among the humans of Jambudvīpa, increase and decrease are discerned. Monks, there are also humans of Jambudvīpa who possess immeasurable lifespans.
Whether their lifespan be eighty thousand years, or a hundred years, or even ten years.

Āps 13. At present, monks, the measure of the lifespan of the humans of Jambudvīpa is one hundred years. At present, monks, among the humans of Jambudvīpa, he who lives long lives for a hundred years or slightly more, being maintained in perfect comfort.
Āps 14. Indeed, monks, while living for a hundred years, one experiences ten stages. In the first stage...

In the first stage, he is a child, dull-witted, and prone to lying on his back. In the second stage, he is a youth, by nature fond of play. In the third stage, he is a young man, an enjoyer of sensual pleasures. In the fourth stage, he is strong and energetic. In the fifth stage, he is wise and possessed of eloquence. In the sixth...

In the [sixth] stage, he is mindful and inclined toward investigation. In the seventh stage, he becomes one who has attained mental stability. In the eighth stage, he becomes an elder among the nobility. In the ninth stage, he becomes old and worn out by age. In the tenth stage, his life-span is gone and he is intent upon death. For a hundred years...
Indeed, monks, one who lives here experiences ten stages.
Monks, indeed, one living for a hundred years lives for three hundred seasons:
a hundred seasons of winter, [a hundred of summer, and a hundred of the rainy season].
A hundred seasons of summer,
a hundred seasons of the rainy season— living for three hundred seasons, one lives for twelve hundred months;
four [hundred] of the winter seasons.
There are four [months] of summer and four of the rainy season. Living for twelve hundred months, he lives for twenty-four hundred half-months.
Eight winters,
eight summers,
and eight rains; living for twenty-four hundred half-months, that is, thirty-six thousand days and nights.
He lives for twelve winters,
twelve summers, and twelve rains.

Living for thirty-six thousand days and nights, one consumes seventy-two thousand meals, including the intervals between meals. These are the interruptions to meals: even when angry, one does not eat.
Though suffering, he does not eat;
though fallen into hardship, he does not eat; though exhausted by hunger, he does not eat.
Even when obtaining food he does not eat; even when not obtaining food he does not eat;
even while asleep he does not eat.
Even when intoxicated he does not eat, and even when negligent he does not eat;
thus, combining together both those who eat and those who do not eat, there are seventy-two thousand meals.
Together with the drinking of my mother’s breast milk. Thus, monks, I have also declared the lifespan of the humans of Jambudvīpa, as well as their seasons.
The months as well, the fortnights as well, and the nights and days as well.
The meals as well as the obstacles to meals have been explained.
Monks, those which are fifty years for humans constitute one night and day for the gods of the Four Great Kings.
By that reckoning of nights and days, thirty such days making a month, and twelve such months making a year,
five hundred divine years by that calculation of years is the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
By human calculation, that constitutes a lifespan of nine million years;
however, there is death in the interim.
That [human lifespan] constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva great hell.
By that reckoning of nights and days— thirty such nights making a month,
and twelve such months making a year—
the beings in the Saṃjīva great hell remain for five hundred years.

The measure of the lifespan of beings is as follows, according to human calculation: the measure of their lifespan is one hundred sixty-two thousand million years (*varṣakoṭīśatasahasra*), yet there is death in the interval. At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Having committed misconduct of body as if it were misconduct of speech,
they are reborn in the Saṃjīva hell because of that karma.

For thousands of millions of years, they live on, being struck down again and again. Men who are obsessed with mutual enmity and who kill other men are reborn in the Saṃjīva hell because of that karma.
Āps 21. Monks, that which is one hundred years for humans is a single day and night for the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven;
by that day and night, with thirty such nights making a month, [and twelve such months making a year].
By a year consisting of twelve months,
and by that calculation of years,
the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven is one thousand divine years. That, by human calculation, amounts to thirty-six million years.
The measure of the lifespan [of the gods] is such that there is death in the interval.
That constitutes one night and day in the great hell Kālasūtra. (Āps 22)
By that reckoning of days and nights— thirty such days making a month,
and twelve such months making a year— the lifespan of the beings in the Kālasūtra great hell is one thousand years. That, in turn, corresponds to [the following] human calculation:
By calculation, the measure of their lifespan is twelve hundred thousand koṭis of years and ninety-six thousand koṭis of years;
however, there is death in the interval.
[Āps 23] Then, at that time, the Blessed One—
He speaks these verses:
"Those who have committed offenses against their mother and father, and against the Buddhas and their disciples, will be reborn in the Kālasūtra hell and experience agonizing sensations. (31)
Those shameless men who cause dissension among friends have fallen into the Kālasūtra hell;
they are liars who speak with deceit.
By that karma, they have fallen into the Kālasūtra hell.
(32) Monks, what constitutes two hundred years for humans is a single day and night for the Yāma gods;
by that day and night...
Thirty nights constitute a month;
twelve months constitute a year. By that calculation of years, the measure of the lifespan of the Yama gods is two thousand divine years. That, in terms of human reckoning, is as follows:
By calculation, the measure of the lifespan is fourteen billion and four million years;
however, there is death in the interim.
That constitutes one day and night in the Saṃghāta great hell.
By that reckoning of days and nights— thirty such nights making a month,
and twelve such months making a year—
in that calculation of years, two thousand years pass for the denizens of the Saṃghāta great hell.
The measure of the lifespan of beings is this: by human calculation, it is one hundred and three billion, six hundred and eighty million years;
such is the measure of their lifespan, though there is death in the interval.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Having committed three kinds of unwholesome deeds, though they have not been performed [by others], they are born in the Saṃghāta hell because of that karma. (33)
Having killed cranes, goats, buffaloes, deer, chickens, pigs, or other living beings, one is reborn in the Saṃghāta hell.
(34) Monks, those four hundred years of human beings constitute a single day and night for the Tuṣita gods. (GBM 1695.2)
By a day and night, thirty such nights constitute a month;
twelve such months constitute a year.
By that calculation of years, the lifespan of the Tuṣita gods is four thousand divine years.
That is the measure. By human calculation, the measure of the lifespan is fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years;
however, there is death in the interval.
That, O monks, is the case in the Raurava great hell.
One night and day; by that night and day, thirty such nights constitute a month;
twelve such months constitute a year.

By that calculation of years, the lifespan of the beings in the great hell Raurava is four thousand years. By human calculation, that constitutes a lifespan of eight quadrillion, twenty-nine trillion,
and forty-four billion years.
There is death in the interval.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The ancient ones were fierce, with blood on their hands..."
Those who habitually practice evil deeds are always born in Raurava;
having destroyed the people, they are burned in Raurava for a long time.
O people, the Tūṭaka and Vaṭika have not emitted the Bhairava roar.
Monks, those which are eight hundred years for humans constitute one day and night for the Nirmāṇarati gods.
By that reckoning of days and nights, thirty such nights making a month,
twelve such months making a year,
and by that calculation of years, there are eight thousand divine years.
The measure of the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati gods is, by human calculation, two hundred and thirty million years and four million years;
this is the measure of their lifespan,
though there is death in the interval.
That constitutes one day and night in the great hell of Mahāraurava;
by thirty such days and nights there is a month, and by twelve such months there is a year. By that [reckoning]...
By calculation of years, the lifespan of the beings in the great hell Mahāraurava is eight thousand years. By human calculation, that constitutes a lifespan of sixty-six quintillion,
three hundred and fifty million, and fifty-two thousand million years.
"There is death in the interval.
(Āps 32) Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Enveloped by the thicket of views, shrouded by the veil of craving and desire..."
Those who practice evil deeds go to the Mahāraurava hell;
having reached Mahāraurava, which is a blazing fire that makes one's hair stand on end, they are burned there.
Bound men who are betrayers of trust,
their limbs severed by swords, are devoured while writhing amidst vultures, crows, owls, and dogs. // 38–39 //

Monks, those which are sixteen hundred years for humans constitute one day and night for the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; by that day and night, with thirty such days making a month, [and twelve such months making a year].
By a year consisting of twelve months,
according to that calculation of years,
[it is] sixteen thousand years.
The measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*) is, by human calculation, twenty-one billion, nine hundred and sixty million years;
this is the measure of their lifespan,
though there is premature death in the interval.
That constitutes one day and night in the Tapanīya great hell; by thirty such days and nights there is a month,
and by twelve such months [there is a year].
By that calculation of years, the lifespan of the beings in the great hell of Tapana is sixteen thousand years. By human reckoning,
that constitutes a lifespan of five hundred and thirty-eight quadrillion, eighty-four trillion, and sixteen billion years.
There is death in the interval.
(Āps 35) Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Śramaṇas, brahmins, virtuous ones, as well as mother and father..."
He who causes suffering by means of refined [metals] falls into the Tapana hell.
Whatever deeds one has performed here that cause many people to suffer, by that karma one is reborn in the Tapana hell. (40–41)
“Bhikṣus, do you wish to hear the limit of the lifespan of beings reborn in Arbuda? Blessed One, this is the time for that; Sugata, this is the occasion for that.”

"May the Blessed One teach the limit of the lifespan of those beings born in the Arbuda hell. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it. "Therefore, monks, listen; attend well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.
"Monks, it is as if there were here a Kosalan sesame-cartload of twenty khārīs, filled with sesame seeds and tied down with a cloth-bag. Then, suppose some man..."

"Monks, if one were to remove a single sesame seed at the end of every hundred years, that Kosalan sesame-cartload consisting of twenty khārīs would indeed be exhausted and come to an end more quickly than I declare to be the limit of the lifespan of beings born in the Arbuda hell."

Āps 38. As twenty *arbudas* are to one *nirarbuda*, so twenty *nirarbudas* are to one *aṭaṭa*. As twenty *aṭaṭas* are to one *hahava*, so twenty *hahavas* are to one *huhuva*. As twenty *huhuvās* are to one *utpala*, so twenty *utpalas* are to one *padma*. As twenty *padmas* are to one *mahāpadma*.
Monks, there Kokālika—who belonged to the faction of Devadatta—having corrupted his mind toward the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, was reborn in the Mahāpadma great hell with his very own body.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: even toward one as small as a speck of dust, we shall not corrupt our minds.
“... much less [should one do so] when consciousness is present. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Regarding verses 42–46, cf. Uv 7.2–6, *Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna*, PatnaDhp 300–303, Sn 127.1–15, SN I 149.17–31, etc.:
"For when a man is born, an axe is born within his mouth."
For by speaking ill words, one cuts oneself with that very speech;
he who praises those who deserve blame and blames those who are worthy of praise.
He gathers that misfortune with his own mouth, by which misfortune he finds no happiness.

For this misfortune is indeed slight, wherein one might lose one's own wealth here through dice; but this is the much greater misfortune herein: that one should harbor a corrupted mind toward the Sugatas.
One hundred thousand and thirty-six plus five *arbuda* hells does one who reviles the noble ones enter,
by means of speech and mind.
Having made an evil vow, those with wicked minds speak untruths; they increase the hells for their own destruction.
One of faultless strength endures them, maintaining the clarity of his mind.
Monks, in the great hell of Pratāpana, the lifespan is half a kalpa;
however, there is death in the interval.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Having abandoned the fruit of merit for the sake of rebirth in heaven..."
Having performed undesirable actions here in this world, they are reborn in the Pratāpana hell.
He who kills ascetics, brahmins, virtuous ones, as well as his mother, father, or other elders, is cooked in the Pratāpana hell.
Monks, the lifespan in the great hell of Avīci is indeed one *kalpa*,
though there may be death before that time. It was there that Devadatta, a deluded man, having split the harmonious Saṅgha,
having shed the blood of the Tathāgata with a malicious mind, and having caused an Arhatī bhikṣuṇī to be killed, was reborn in the great hell of Avīci with his very own body.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The one of dull intellect who, relying on an evil view, reviles the teaching of the noble Arhats who live according to the Dharma— "
The thorny bamboo bears fruit that leads to its own destruction.
One should release only a virtuous woman, but never a wicked one;
for while it is better to release a virtuous woman, releasing a wicked one brings remorse.
If one should release it or fasten it again, by releasing it, one is bound.
The noble ones do not release that [bond]; the fools release themselves through evil deeds.
Having performed here such actions that lead to an evil rebirth... (51) adhi... having performed such actions here, one goes to a miserable state.
By that karma, they are reborn in the Avīci hell.
Monks, the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika gods is half an eon (*ardhakalpa*),
though there is death in the interval.
Āps 46. Monks, the lifespan of the Brahma-purohita devas is one kalpa; however, there is death in the interval. Āps 47. Monks, the lifespan of the Mahābrahmā devas is one and a half kalpas.
One and a half kalpas.
The measure of the lifespan [of the Parīttābha gods] is two eons;
however, there is death in the interval.
Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Parīttābha gods is two eons; however, there is death in the interval. (Āps 48)
Monks, the lifespan of the gods of the Apramāṇābha heaven is four kalpas,
though there is death in the interval.
Āps 50. Monks, the lifespan of the Ābhāsvara gods is eight eons; however, there is death in the interval. Āps 51. [The lifespan] of the Parīttāśubha gods...
Monks, the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is sixteen kalpas;
there is, however, death in the interval.
Monks, the lifespan of the gods of the Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha) is thirty-two kalpas.
There is death in the interval.
Monks, the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna gods is sixty-four eons,
yet there is death in the interval.
Āps 54. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Anabhraka gods is one hundred and twenty-five eons; there is, however, death in the interval.
Āps 55. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Puṇyaprasava gods is two hundred and fifty eons.
There is death in the interval. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Bṛhatphala gods is five hundred kalpas.
There is death in the interval.
(Āps 57) Likewise, for the non-percipient beings, the measure of the lifespan is five hundred eons,
yet there is death in the interval.
"Monks, the lifespan of the Abṛha gods is one thousand kalpas;
however, there is death in the interval."
"Monks, the lifespan of the Atapa devas is two thousand kalpas;
there is, however, death in the interval.
Monks, the lifespan of the Sudṛśa devas is four thousand kalpas."
There is death in the interval.
Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the Sudarśana gods is eight thousand kalpas; there is death in the interval.
Āps 62. Monks, the lifespan of the Akaniṣṭha gods is sixteen thousand kalpas; there is, however, death in the interval.
Āps 63. Monks, the lifespan of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) is twenty thousand kalpas.
There is death in the interval. Monks, the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness is forty thousand eons;
there is death in the interval.
Āps 65. Monks, the lifespan of the gods of the sphere of nothingness is sixty thousand eons;
however, there is death in the interval.
Āps 66. Monks, the lifespan of the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is eighty thousand eons.
There is death in the interval.
